title: Centre-Restart Conversion Simulation
primarySkill: Converting centre-clearance possession into an effective forward entry.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to win, receive or recover possession from a centre restart and convert it into a controlled scoring opportunity while maintaining protection against turnover.
groundSize: Centre square to the attacking goal, using approximately half to two-thirds of a full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two teams around a centre restart, including rucks, inside midfielders, wings, half-forwards, key forwards and defenders.
Begin each repetition with a ball-up or controlled ruck contest in the centre circle.
The attacking team scores through a goal, behind or marked possession inside 30 metres.
The defending team scores by winning possession and moving the football beyond the centre square or through designated wide exit gates.
Place one spare football with the coach for rapid resets.
Rotate starting midfield combinations every three to four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach restarts play with a centre ball-up.
Both teams contest possession using their normal centre-restart structures.
The team winning the clearance attempts to create a purposeful forward entry rather than immediately kicking without assessing options.
Forwards may lead at the football, hold deeper space or create separation for a teammate.
If the defending team wins possession, play continues live as it attempts to exit through the centre or wide gates.
Award three points for a goal, two points for a marked possession inside 30 metres and one point for an uncontested inside-50 possession.
Award the defensive team two points for a clean turnover and successful exit.
Stop the repetition after a score, defensive exit, stoppage lasting more than five seconds or the football leaves the designated area.
Reset quickly and repeat from the centre.
coachingPoints: Midfielders must scan before the ruck contest and understand the likely hit zone.
The first possession should create time and space for the next disposal rather than forcing an immediate clearance.
Outside midfielders must hold width until possession is established.
Forwards should coordinate leads so that multiple players do not attack the same space.
The ball carrier should identify whether the best option is a direct corridor entry, a wide release or a controlled possession.
Players behind the football must protect against a turnover and immediate counterattack.
Communication must begin before the ball-up and continue through the entire passage.
After a lost clearance, all players must react immediately and defend the next possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders adjust their starting positions to the nominated or developing hit zone.
Whether the clearance winner has support forward, lateral and behind.
Whether forwards create multiple usable lanes rather than leading into congestion.
Whether the inside-50 kick is selected according to pressure and forward positioning.
Whether defenders and midfielders react immediately when possession changes.
Whether the team maintains a balanced structure behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders all chase the football into the same space.
commonErrors.correction: Assign clear hit-zone, receiver and defensive-side roles before each restart.

commonErrors.error: The clearance is kicked forward without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require the ball carrier to identify a target or release option before disposing.

commonErrors.error: Forwards lead toward the same corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate separate lead lanes and demand early communication.

commonErrors.error: Wings collapse too early into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the team has clearly won or lost possession.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after losing the clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Continue every repetition until the opposition exits or a stoppage is called.

progressions: Allow the defending team to launch a full counterattack toward the opposite goal.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios before each centre restart.
Require the attacking side to use a nominated forward-entry method, then remove the restriction.
Start some repetitions with an unexpected ruck hit or loose football.
Allow coaches to change midfield match-ups between repetitions.
regressions: Begin with an uncontested ruck hit to a nominated midfielder.
Reduce the number of defenders in the forward half.
Limit play to one centre-clearance method at a time.
Use controlled contact and slower resets.
Mark preferred forward-entry lanes with cones.
successIndicators: Establish clear roles before the centre restart.
Win or neutralise first possession without overcommitting.
Create a controlled inside-50 entry from the clearance.
Provide width, depth and forward support.
Generate a shot, mark or strong contest inside 50.
React immediately when the opposition wins possession.
matchApplication: This drill replicates the moments immediately after a centre bounce, when teams must convert a clearance into a scoring opportunity while remaining prepared for an opposition win. It develops the connection between the ruck, midfield, wings and forwards and reinforces the importance of attacking with structure rather than relying on rushed territory kicks.

title: Forward-Half Lock-In and Defensive Exit Simulation
Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation
Match-Simulation Foundation Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating foundational match-simulation behaviours across continuous and varied phases.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently apply the foundational match-simulation behaviours developed in MS-001 to MS-019 across connected phases of live Australian football.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with full positional roles.
Establish a scoreboard and countdown clock.
Prepare six starting scenarios covering defensive intercept, kick-mark possession, corridor access, wing contest, forward entry and stoppage.
Assign coaches to observe specific team behaviours.
Play three blocks of eight to ten minutes.
Use minimal coach intervention during each block.
Begin each block from a different scenario.
Require player leaders to organise feedback between blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the first starting scenario.
Teams organise and begin live play.
After the initial phase, play continues without restriction.
Coaches assess structure, decision making, communication, skill execution and transition.
Natural stoppages and turnovers are played under normal match conditions.
At the end of the block, teams receive a two-minute player-led review.
The second block begins from a different phase and scoreboard condition.
The final block begins without the scenario being announced until players reach the starting position.
Award points for the match score and nominated tactical behaviours.
Finish with individual and team ratings against the success indicators.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise the current phase without waiting for coach instruction.
The team should maintain balance between possession, territory and attacking risk.
Defensive structures must remain connected behind the football.
The first possession after a contest or turnover must have purpose.
Forward entries should match the available options.
Restarts require immediate organisation.
Communication should continue throughout all phases.
Players must apply feedback from earlier blocks.
Coaches should assess repeatability, not isolated successful moments.

commonErrors.error: Players perform well only in the announced starting phase.
commonErrors.correction: Continue assessing structure after play becomes unpredictable.

commonErrors.error: Teams rely on coaches to organise restarts.
commonErrors.correction: Require player leaders to call roles and match-ups.

commonErrors.error: Attacking numbers move ahead of the football without protection.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain connected support behind possession.

commonErrors.error: Forward entries are rushed after long possession chains.
commonErrors.correction: Reassess the forward structure before the final disposal.

commonErrors.error: Feedback does not transfer into later blocks.
commonErrors.correction: Assign a player leader responsibility for reinforcing the correction.

progressions: Play a full quarter without coach interruption.
Add interchange restrictions and fatigue.
Use hidden scoreboard objectives for each team.
Record the simulation for detailed tactical review.
Require players to complete self-assessment before coach feedback.
regressions: Use four starting scenarios rather than six.
Shorten playing blocks.
Pause briefly before major restarts.
Reduce ground size and player numbers.
Provide player leaders with tactical reminder cards.
successIndicators: Recognise and organise for changing match phases.
Use the corridor without forcing risk.
Connect stoppage wins to attacking outcomes.
matchApplication: This assessment completes the foundational stage of the Match Simulation chapter. It tests whether players can combine restart organisation, possession control, contest work, transition, forward connection and defensive response within continuous football rather than treating each skill as an isolated exercise.
relatedDrills: MS-013 – Corridor Access and Release Simulation

title: High-Ball Defensive Exit Contest Simulation
primarySkill: Exiting defensive territory through a structured high-ball contest.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to organise a long defensive exit, create a competitive aerial contest and control the secondary possession around the target.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 25 metres beyond the centre.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in possession inside defensive 50.
Establish a long marking target near the wing or centre.
Position aerial defenders and ground-level players around the target.
Mark front, rear, inside and boundary-side support zones.
Position one defensive-cover player behind the contest.
The exiting team attempts to gain territory or retain possession.
The opposition attempts to intercept and return the football inside 50.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team begins with possession inside 50.
Short options are initially pressured, encouraging consideration of a long exit.
The ball carrier selects a high-ball target.
The aerial players compete to mark, neutralise or direct the football.
Ground-level players contest the secondary possession.
The exiting team attempts to cross a forward territory line.
Award three points for a mark followed by controlled forward possession.
Award two points for winning the spill and crossing the territory line.
Award one point for creating a forward stoppage.
Award the opposition three points for an intercept or clean return entry.
coachingPoints: The long target must provide a genuine contest rather than stand underneath the football.
Ground-level roles should include front, rear, inside and defensive-side coverage.
The kick should favour the target’s protected side.
Players must anticipate the likely spoil direction.
The team should recognise when a forward stoppage is an acceptable result.
Defensive-cover players must remain connected behind the contest.
If the secondary possession is won, players should spread immediately.
The kicker must avoid choosing an isolated target surrounded by opposition numbers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Selection and positioning of the long target.
Direction of marks, spoils and spills.

commonErrors.error: The target waits flat-footed under the football.
commonErrors.correction: Approach the contest with momentum and strong body position.

commonErrors.error: All ground-level players stand front and centre.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate front, back, inside and defensive-side roles.

commonErrors.error: The kick is placed to the defender’s advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football to the target’s protected side.

commonErrors.error: Players treat a forward stoppage as failure.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise territory and a reset as a positive defensive outcome.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a connected defensive-cover player.

progressions: Add a second aerial target and defender.
Allow the opposition to vary its press.
Continue play to the opposite goal after winning the secondary possession.
Begin with the exiting team outnumbered around the contest.
Add a scoreboard scenario requiring possession rather than territory.
regressions: Use a controlled kick to a nominated target area.
Reduce aerial contact.
Remove one opposition ground-level player.
Mark support zones clearly.
Stop after the aerial contest to coach secondary positioning.
successIndicators: Transition quickly after winning the secondary ball.
matchApplication: Teams frequently need to escape defensive pressure through a long kick. Success depends on the organisation around the contest rather than the kick alone.
relatedDrills: MS-014 – Wing Contest and Secondary Possession Simulation

title: Forward-50 Repeat Tackle Chain Simulation
primarySkill: Creating consecutive legal tackle and pressure actions inside attacking 50.
objective: Develop the forward group’s ability to continue pressure after the first tackle attempt, close the next receiver and convert repeat defensive actions into scoring opportunities.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position defenders with possession inside defensive 50.
Position forwards in a connected pressure structure.
Mark central and wide defensive exit gates.
Begin with a defender receiving a ground ball or handball under pressure.
The defensive team attempts to complete an exit chain.
The forwards attempt to tackle, force a rushed disposal or regain possession.
Rotate first pressure, cover and interceptor roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach releases the football to a defender.
The nearest forward closes and attempts a legal tackle or pressure action.
If the football is released, the next forward pressures the receiver.
Other forwards guard central and wide exits.
The chain continues until the defenders exit, turn the football over or create a stoppage.
Award the forward team one point for each effective pressure action.
Award three points for a tackle or turnover that produces a goal.
Award two points for forcing a stoppage inside 50.
Award the defensive team three points for a controlled exit.
Reset with a different starting defender and pressure angle.
coachingPoints: Tacklers must close under control and protect their head.
The first pressure player should direct the ball carrier toward support.
The next forward must anticipate the likely release.
Players should complete tackles legally and avoid sling actions.
Support forwards must guard dangerous exits rather than spectate.
Players who miss a tackle must recover into the next pressure action.
After a turnover, the team should spread enough to create a quality scoring option.
Communication must identify pressure, cover and free opponents.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Direction created by the first pressure player.
Quality of the scoring decision after a regain.

commonErrors.error: Tacklers arrive too fast and are evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate, balance and close the ball carrier’s space.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football rather than the next receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Anticipate where the disposal is likely to go.

commonErrors.error: Missed tacklers remain on the ground or stop.
commonErrors.correction: Regain feet immediately and join the next pressure action.

commonErrors.error: Tackles become unsafe under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce legal technique and reduce intensity when control is lost.

commonErrors.error: Players rush the scoring disposal after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and identify the best scoring option.

progressions: Increase defensive support numbers.
Reduce the size of the exit area.
Begin with the forwards temporarily outnumbered.
Add repeated possessions without reset.
Introduce a scoreboard condition requiring a goal.
regressions: Use controlled tackling.
Reduce defender numbers.
Limit defensive exits to one side.
Begin with a known first receiver.
Pause between pressure actions to coach roles.
successIndicators: Direct the ball carrier toward support.
Force stoppages, turnovers or rushed exits.
Convert pressure wins into quality scoring chances.
matchApplication: Forward pressure often requires several consecutive tackle and chase efforts. This simulation develops the connected pressure chain needed to prevent defensive exits.
relatedDrills: MS-053 – Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation

title: Pressure and Contest Development Stage Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating advanced pressure, contest, recovery and resilience behaviours across continuous match phases.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently apply the advanced pressure and contest behaviours developed in MS-041 to MS-059 during continuous, varied and physically demanding match simulation.
equipment: Towels and spare dry footballs if wet-weather conditions are included
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with interchange players.
Prepare six scenario cards covering defensive siege, long defensive exit, forward pressure, midfield turnover, defensive stoppage and broken play.
Include one block using a damp football or wet-weather decision constraints if conditions are safe.
Assign coaches specific pressure and contest behaviours to assess.
Establish a scoreboard and countdown clock.
Play three blocks of ten to twelve minutes.
Use short player-led reviews between blocks.
Maintain normal match rules and safe contact standards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the first starting scenario.
Teams organise and begin live play.
Once the initial phase ends, play continues normally.
Coaches assess pressure angles, contest roles, recovery positioning, communication and decision quality.
At unpredictable moments, the coach introduces a new scenario through a restart or replacement football.
Teams must adapt without a full tactical reset.
At the end of each block, players complete a two-minute review identifying one strength and one priority correction.
Award points for normal match scoring and nominated pressure behaviours.
The final block includes consecutive contest phases under accumulated fatigue.
Conclude with individual, line and team ratings against the success indicators.
coachingPoints: Pressure must protect dangerous space and influence the next disposal.
Players around contests must maintain distinct roles.
Defensive teams must reset quickly during repeated opposition entries.
Long exits require aerial and ground-level organisation.
Counter-pressure must begin immediately after turnovers.
Repeated tackling must remain legal and technically sound.
Players must identify and restore structure during broken play.
Territory and stoppages may be valuable outcomes in difficult conditions.
Fatigue must not remove communication or tactical discipline.
Coaches should assess consistency across the entire session rather than isolated highlights.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Adaptation to wet or difficult footballs.

commonErrors.error: Players apply pressure individually without team connection.
commonErrors.correction: Coordinate the first pressure action with coverage of the next options.

commonErrors.error: Contest numbers arrive without defined responsibilities.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate ball-winner, protector, receiver, pressure and cover roles.

commonErrors.error: Defensive structure fails after repeated efforts.
commonErrors.correction: Reset goal-side, corridor and exit responsibilities after every phase.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue creates rushed disposals or unsafe contact.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify decisions and reduce load when technique deteriorates.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to adapt when conditions or scenarios change.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the current phase and adjust possession, territory and risk.

progressions: Play a full quarter without coach interruption.
Use hidden tactical objectives for each team.
Reduce interchange availability.
Add final-minute scoreboard and time pressure.
Record the assessment for detailed line and player review.
regressions: Use four scenarios rather than six.
Shorten playing blocks.
Increase recovery between blocks.
Pause before major scenario changes.
Provide player leaders with contest-role reminder cards.
successIndicators: Reset defensive structure during repeated entries.
Organise aerial and ground-level exit support.
Select possession, territory or stoppage appropriately.
Maintain technique and communication under fatigue.
Adapt to changing conditions and scenarios.
Perform pressure and contest behaviours without continuous coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment completes the pressure-and-contest development stage of the Match Simulation chapter. It determines whether players can transfer contest structure, defensive resilience, forward pressure, turnover response and fatigue discipline into continuous match-like football.MS-061 – Defensive-Half Possession Launch Simulation
relatedDrills: MS-052 – High-Ball Defensive Exit Contest Simulation
MS-053 – Ground-Level Forward Pressure Wave Simulation

title: Half-Forward Outlet and Inside-50 Re-Entry Simulation
Defensive-50 Overload-to-Release Simulation
primarySkill: Creating and using a numerical overload to escape defensive 50.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to create a temporary numerical advantage around defensive possession, draw opposition pressure and release the football into open space.
groundSize: Defensive goal line to approximately 25 metres beyond defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one team in possession inside defensive 50.
Organise the opposition in a forward-half press.
Mark one overload zone on the starting side and three exit gates beyond defensive 50.
Allow the possession team one additional player inside the overload zone.
Position far-side defenders, wings and midfielders as release options.
Begin each repetition with a mark, free kick or controlled ground-ball possession.
Rotate the overload side and initial ball carrier.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team begins with possession inside the overload zone.
Nearby teammates create short and lateral options to attract opposition pressure.
The possession team attempts to involve the spare player without becoming crowded.
Once the opposition commits numbers, the ball carrier releases to the far side, corridor or advancing wing.
The team attempts to exit defensive 50 through a designated gate.
Award three points for a central exit created from the overload.
Award two points for a controlled wide exit.
Award the pressing team three points for a turnover and scoring opportunity.
Continue until an exit, turnover, score or stoppage.
Reset from the opposite side.
coachingPoints: The overload should create an extra option rather than extra congestion.
Players must maintain different depths and angles.
The ball carrier should draw pressure before releasing.
The spare player should be positioned where one defender cannot cover two options.
The far-side release must remain available.
Players should accelerate once the press has been displaced.
Support behind the football must remain connected.
Communication should identify the spare player and the intended release side.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the overload creates usable space.
Support after the first exit possession.

commonErrors.error: Too many players enter the overload zone.
commonErrors.correction: Use only the numbers required to create one clear spare.

commonErrors.error: Players stand at the same depth.
commonErrors.correction: Stagger short, lateral and long options.

commonErrors.error: The football is released before the press commits.
commonErrors.correction: Draw an opponent before transferring possession.

commonErrors.error: The far side moves toward the overload.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain width until the release begins.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after escaping the first pressure line.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting until the football has exited defensive 50.

progressions: Remove the numerical advantage after the first disposal.
Allow the opposition to change pressing structures.
Continue play to the opposite goal.
Introduce a six-second decision limit.
Begin with the possession team under immediate physical pressure.
regressions: Increase the possession team’s overload to two spare players.
Reduce opposition pressure.
Widen the exit gates.
Predetermine the release side.
Pause after the first possession to organise spacing.
successIndicators: Maintain effective spacing around the overload.
matchApplication: Defensive teams often create exits by bringing an extra player to the ball side, attracting pressure and releasing the football elsewhere. This simulation develops the spacing and decision making required to use that advantage effectively.

title: Boundary Compression-to-Open-Side Release Simulation
primarySkill: Escaping boundary congestion by transferring possession to the open side.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to draw opposition numbers toward a boundary contest, secure possession and transfer the football to open space on the opposite side.
groundSize: A boundary channel connected to the full opposite half of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Begin with a boundary contest involving several players from both teams.
Position open-side wings, defenders and midfielders away from the congestion.
Mark one central and one wide open-side release gate.
The possession team attempts to secure the football and transfer away from the boundary.
The defending team attempts to trap possession or intercept the switch.
Rotate boundary and open-side roles.
Vary the starting field position.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts a live boundary contest or throw-in.
Both teams compete for possession.
The team winning the football creates a short release away from immediate pressure.
Open-side players maintain width and adjust their depth.
The football is transferred through a kick, handball chain or switch possession.
The receiving player attacks through an open-side gate.
Award three points for a controlled open-side release.
Award two points for escaping the boundary through the corridor.
Award the defending team three points for trapping the football or intercepting the transfer.
Reset from a different boundary location.
coachingPoints: The first possession should escape immediate pressure rather than force a long switch.
Open-side players must remain available and visible.
Support around the contest should create a release angle.
The team should move the football quickly once the open side becomes available.
The switch kick must favour the receiver.
Players behind possession must protect against an intercepted transfer.
The far-side receiver should scan before the football arrives.
A repeat boundary stoppage remains acceptable when no safe release exists.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Release support around the boundary contest.
Width and depth of open-side players.
Timing and accuracy of the transfer.

commonErrors.error: The first possession attempts a long switch under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Create a short release before transferring the football.

commonErrors.error: Open-side players move toward the congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until possession is secured.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand directly behind the ball winner.
commonErrors.correction: Create lateral and backward release angles.

commonErrors.error: The switch hangs in the air and allows recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Use a flatter, accurate kick to the receiver’s advantage.

commonErrors.error: Players force the release when trapped.
commonErrors.correction: Protect possession and accept the stoppage.

progressions: Reduce the space available around the boundary contest.
Add a recovering defender on the open side.
Continue the release to a full scoring opportunity.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios where territory is critical.
Begin with the possession team outnumbered at the contest.
regressions: Use controlled contact at the boundary contest.
Remove one opposition open-side defender.
Predetermine the release sequence.
Widen the open-side gates.
Pause after possession is secured.
successIndicators: Secure or neutralise the boundary contest.
Create an initial release from congestion.
Attack the open side at speed.
matchApplication: Boundary contests often draw most players toward one side of the ground. Teams that secure possession and access the opposite side can attack before the opposition recovers.

title: Full-Ground Overlap Chain Simulation
primarySkill: Creating and sustaining overlap support across multiple lines of the ground.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to create consecutive overlap runs from defence through midfield and into attack while preserving support behind the football.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one team in defensive possession.
Organise opposition pressure across defensive, midfield and forward lines.
Place potential overlap runners behind and lateral to the initial ball carrier.
Position midfielders and forwards to continue the overlap chain.
Begin with an intercept or controlled defensive possession.
The attacking team attempts to complete at least three connected overlap actions.
The opposition attempts to delay, intercept or counterattack.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defensive team begins with possession.
The first overlap runner moves past or outside the ball carrier.
The ball carrier draws pressure and releases.
The receiving player connects with the next overlap or forward option.
Additional runners join from midfield and half-forward.
The team attempts to create a scoring opportunity.
Award one point for each successful overlap action.
Award three points for a controlled inside-50 entry.
Award five points for a goal following three or more overlaps.
Reset after a score, turnover, stoppage or defensive exit.
coachingPoints: Overlap runners should attack space rather than run directly beside the ball carrier.
The ball carrier must draw an opponent before releasing.
Runners should stagger their timing.
Players who dispose must continue supporting the chain.
A kicking option should remain available when handball pressure becomes excessive.
Support behind the football must remain connected.
Forwards should respond to the speed and direction of the overlap.
After turnover, runners must recover through the corridor.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Angles and timing of overlap runs.
Whether the ball carrier draws pressure.

commonErrors.error: Overlap runners move too close to the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Run wider or beyond to create separation.

commonErrors.error: Multiple runners arrive simultaneously.
commonErrors.correction: Stagger the first, second and third overlap efforts.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier releases before pressure commits.
commonErrors.correction: Carry directly at the defender before disposing.

commonErrors.error: The chain relies only on handball.
commonErrors.correction: Retain kicking options when the defence compresses.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after giving the football.
commonErrors.correction: Continue to the next support or coverage position.

progressions: Increase defender numbers.
Require the final entry to produce a goal.
Begin with the attacking team under immediate pressure.
Allow full contact and live counterattack.
Add a second transition immediately after a turnover.
regressions: Use passive defenders.
Predetermine the first two overlap runners.
Reduce the ground length.
Delay opposition recovery.
Allow an uncontested first possession.
successIndicators: Create overlap support across multiple lines.
Connect the overlap to a scoring opportunity.
matchApplication: Damaging transition often requires several overlap efforts rather than one isolated run. This simulation develops continuous support from defence to attack.

title: Forward-Half Possession Lock and Switch Simulation
Defensive Line-Break Prevention and Rebound Simulation
Inside-50 Possession Retention and Shot Creation Simulation
Team Ball Movement Development Stage Assessment
Consecutive-Goal Momentum Reset Simulation
primarySkill: Resetting team structure and behaviour after conceding consecutive goals.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to respond calmly and structurally after conceding consecutive goals, stabilise possession and prevent an opposition scoring run from continuing.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams.
Begin with one team recorded as having conceded two consecutive goals.
Restart from the centre square.
Give the recovering team 15 seconds to communicate its reset plan.
The opposition attempts to maintain momentum and score again.
Use a five-minute scenario clock.
Rotate which team manages the momentum reset.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces that one team has conceded two consecutive goals.
Player leaders call the immediate centre-restart and possession plan.
Play restarts from the centre.
The recovering team attempts to win or neutralise the clearance and establish controlled possession.
The opposition applies aggressive pressure to continue its scoring run.
Play continues for five minutes or until one team achieves a nominated outcome.
Award the recovering team three points for preventing another goal and establishing possession.
Award two points for forcing a neutral stoppage or territory gain after the restart.
Award the momentum team three points for scoring another goal.
Review the emotional and tactical response before repeating.
coachingPoints: Players must move immediately from frustration to the next responsibility.
The reset plan should be simple and clearly communicated.
Winning the next possession may be more important than forcing an immediate score.
Centre-square roles must remain disciplined despite emotional pressure.
Players should avoid overcommitting numbers forward.
The team may use possession and territory to reduce opposition momentum.
Leaders must reinforce composure through actions and communication.
One successful defensive or possession phase should become the foundation for normal play.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Emotional response after the scenario announcement.
Decision quality during the first possession.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt to recover the score immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Stabilise possession and field position first.

commonErrors.error: Emotional frustration creates undisciplined centre-square movement.
commonErrors.correction: Return to clear ruck, inside and outside roles.

commonErrors.error: Too many players move ahead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain balance and protection behind possession.

commonErrors.error: Players stop communicating after another error.
commonErrors.correction: Leaders must reinforce the next action immediately.

commonErrors.error: Possession is rushed because the team feels under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use simple, high-percentage options to regain control.

progressions: Begin after conceding three consecutive goals.
Start with the opposition already holding midfield possession.
Add a narrow scoreboard margin and limited time.
Remove coach communication completely.
Require the recovering team to stabilise before attacking for a score.
regressions: Begin with the recovering team in controlled possession.
Increase the scenario time.
Reduce opposition pressure.
Pause after the centre clearance to discuss the reset.
Provide the team with a pre-planned momentum response.
successIndicators: Win, neutralise or pressure the next possession.
matchApplication: Consecutive opposition goals can create emotional and tactical instability. This simulation teaches teams to interrupt momentum through composure, structure and purposeful possession.

title: Forward-Half Stoppage Set-Play Simulation
primarySkill: Executing planned attacking methods from forward-half stoppages.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to organise and execute multiple forward-half stoppage methods while maintaining protection against an opposition clearance.
groundSize: Inside attacking 50 and approximately 20 metres outside the arc.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position rucks, midfielders, forwards and defenders around forward-half stoppages.
Prepare three to five attacking set plays.
Include boundary throw-ins, ball-ups and stoppages near the forward arc.
Assign defensive players realistic match-up and space responsibilities.
Position one or two attacking players outside the immediate stoppage for rebound prevention.
Rotate ruck and midfield combinations.
Allow the defending team to counterattack after winning possession.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces or signals the attacking stoppage method.
Players organise roles before the restart.
The ruck and midfielders execute the intended hit, movement or release.
Forwards create space for the nominated scoring option.
If the initial method fails, play continues live.
The defending team attempts to win possession and exit defensive 50.
Award three points for a shot created directly from the set play.
Award four points for a goal from the method.
Award the defending team three points for winning the stoppage and exiting.
Reset from a different stoppage position and method.
coachingPoints: Players must understand the purpose of the set play, not only their movement.
Ruck and midfield timing must be precise.
Forwards should create space rather than crowd the intended exit.
Ground-level coverage must account for an imperfect hit.
Players outside the stoppage should protect against defensive release.
The team must transition to normal play if the set method fails.
Different methods should be available for different field positions.
Communication should disguise intent where possible.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Timing between ruck and midfield movement.
Ability to continue after the set play breaks down.

commonErrors.error: Players memorise movement without understanding the objective.
commonErrors.correction: Explain the scoring space or receiver the method is designed to create.

commonErrors.error: Forwards crowd the planned exit.
commonErrors.correction: Clear the target area before the restart.

commonErrors.error: The ruck hit is treated as guaranteed.
commonErrors.correction: Position for neutral and opposition outcomes.

commonErrors.error: Players stop when the set play fails.
commonErrors.correction: Transition immediately into normal pressure and structure.

commonErrors.error: No one protects against a defensive clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain players outside and behind the stoppage.

progressions: Allow the defence to scout and adjust to the set play.
Use disguised calls and late changes.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require players to select the method without coach input.
Continue full-ground play after defensive exits.
regressions: Walk through the movement before live execution.
Use controlled ruck contests.
Reduce defensive numbers.
Practise one method from one position.
Pause after the hit to coach forward movement.
successIndicators: Continue playing when the method fails.
matchApplication: Forward-half stoppages offer opportunities to create planned scoring methods. Their value depends on role clarity, timing and the ability to transition when the planned outcome does not occur.

title: Injury and Emergency Role Reallocation Simulation
Match-Day Interchange Load Management Simulation
primarySkill: Managing interchanges to maintain player work rate and positional structure.
objective: Develop players and coaches’ ability to complete planned and reactive interchanges while maintaining team balance, role coverage and safe physical workloads.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground with a marked interchange area.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams with interchange players.
Prepare planned rotation chains for midfield, wing, forward and defensive roles.
Establish maximum playing blocks appropriate to age and conditioning.
Nominate an interchange manager for each team.
Begin a continuous quarter.
Coaches may call planned or reactive rotations.
Player safety and individual restrictions override the drill objectives.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins from a centre restart.
Interchange managers track player time and planned rotations.
Players communicate when approaching their nominated rotation period.
Outgoing players complete role and match-up handovers.
Incoming players enter with immediate awareness of the current phase.
Coaches may create an unplanned rotation due to simulated fatigue, match-up need or tactical change.
Play continues without drill stoppages.
Award two points for completing each clean rotation chain.
Deduct one behaviour point for a vacant role, duplicated change or interchange communication error.
Review workload balance and structural effects after the quarter.
coachingPoints: Rotations should support performance rather than occur blindly according to a clock.
Players must communicate fatigue honestly and early.
Planned rotation chains should preserve positional coverage.
Outgoing players must hand over direct opponents.
Incoming players should understand the match phase before entering.
Multiple connected players should not leave simultaneously unless planned.
Coaches should monitor individual conditioning, age and return-to-play restrictions.
The team must maintain scoreboard and tactical awareness during rotations.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Communication of fatigue and replacement needs.
Impact of rotations on team performance.

commonErrors.error: Players wait until exhausted before requesting rotation.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate early enough to complete an organised change.

commonErrors.error: Several midfielders rotate simultaneously.
commonErrors.correction: Use staggered rotation chains.

commonErrors.error: Outgoing players leave without handing over opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm responsibility before exiting.

commonErrors.error: Incoming players focus on finding a position rather than current play.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the ball, opponent and team structure before entering.

commonErrors.error: Rotation plans ignore the match situation.
commonErrors.correction: Delay or modify changes when a critical phase requires continuity.

progressions: Reduce interchange availability.
Introduce a restricted total interchange count.
Add specific player-minute targets.
Require player leaders to manage rotations.
Play two consecutive quarters and compare workload distribution.
regressions: Use fixed rotation times.
Pause briefly for early rotation chains.
Reduce the number of positional rotations.
Provide clear written rotation maps.
Play shorter blocks.
matchApplication: Effective interchange management supports physical performance and tactical stability. Poorly organised rotations can create structural gaps even when player workloads are well intended.
relatedDrills: MS-039 – Interchange and Positional Rotation Simulation

title: Ground-Dimension Tactical Adaptation Simulation
primarySkill: Adapting team structure and ball movement to different ground dimensions.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to adjust spacing, movement and tactical priorities when playing on grounds that are wider, narrower, longer or shorter than its usual venue.
groundSize: Two or more differently proportioned playing areas marked within the available ground.
equipment: Goal posts or portable scoring posts
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark one narrow playing area and one wide playing area.
Where space permits, also vary ground length.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare tactical objectives for each ground shape.
Play one block in each marked area.
Maintain realistic positional spacing within each shape.
Explain all boundaries clearly before beginning.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins in the first ground configuration.
Teams adjust their structures to the available width and length.
The coach observes corridor access, boundary use, defensive shifting and forward spacing.
Play continues for six to eight minutes.
Teams move to the second ground configuration.
Players identify the required tactical changes before play resumes.
Award behaviour points for correct use of space.
Award normal match points for scoring.
Compare ball movement and defensive structure between configurations.
Finish with a player-led discussion of the tactical differences.
coachingPoints: Narrow grounds increase congestion and the value of boundary territory.
Wide grounds increase switching opportunities and defensive running demands.
Longer grounds require stronger line connection and repeat running.
Shorter grounds increase the danger of turnovers close to goal.
Forward spacing must reflect available width and depth.
Defensive lines should adjust their lateral and vertical separation.
Players must understand the dimensions before the match begins.
Tactical adaptation should not remove fundamental team principles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Team width in each ground shape.

commonErrors.error: Players use normal spacing regardless of ground width.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust lateral positions to the available space.

commonErrors.error: Teams force corridor play on a narrow ground.
commonErrors.correction: Use boundary territory and contest support when central space is congested.

commonErrors.error: Far-side options are ignored on a wide ground.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve width and use switches to move the opposition.

commonErrors.error: Positional lines become disconnected on a long ground.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce gaps and increase linking movement.

commonErrors.error: Players are unaware of shortened scoring distance.
commonErrors.correction: Protect turnovers and adjust shot selection.

progressions: Conceal the next ground shape until the teams arrive.
Change dimensions during a playing block.
Add wind-direction considerations.
Remove coach instruction and require player-led adaptation.
Use a full quarter on an unfamiliar venue.
regressions: Use only narrow and wide configurations.
Pause before play to map positional changes.
Reduce opposition pressure.
Mark preferred lanes visibly.
Use shorter playing blocks.
successIndicators: Recognise the tactical effect of ground dimensions.
Adjust team width and line spacing.
Apply core team principles in different spaces.
matchApplication: Ground dimensions vary significantly across Australian football venues. Teams that adjust their spacing and strategy can use unfamiliar dimensions as an advantage rather than a disruption.

title: Player-Led Match Simulation Review
primarySkill: Leading the observation, review and adjustment of team performance during match simulation.
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify performance patterns, deliver constructive feedback and implement team adjustments with minimal coach direction.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams.
Nominate player leadership groups for each team.
Assign non-playing or rotating players specific observation roles.
Prepare three match-simulation blocks of six to eight minutes.
Coaches remain observers unless safety or major misunderstanding requires intervention.
Player leaders conduct all between-block reviews.
Use a scoreboard and clear tactical objectives.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin the first live match-simulation block.
Player observers record specific examples of team behaviours.
At the end of the block, leadership groups conduct a two-minute review.
Players identify one strength, one problem and one adjustment.
Leaders assign responsibilities for the next block.
Coaches do not add feedback unless invited or required for safety.
The second and third blocks test whether the adjustment is applied.
Observers measure the selected behaviour.
Teams finish with a player-led full-group review.
Coaches provide a final assessment of the review process rather than controlling its content.
coachingPoints: Player feedback must be specific and behaviour based.
Leaders should invite information from different positional lines.
Reviews should remain brief and focused.
The selected adjustment must assign clear responsibilities.
Players should distinguish structural, skill and effort problems.
Positive behaviours should be reinforced.
Feedback must remain respectful and constructive.
The next block should provide evidence of whether the adjustment worked.

commonErrors.error: Reviews become general motivational speeches.
commonErrors.correction: Identify a specific behaviour, example and correction.

commonErrors.error: Only senior leaders contribute.
commonErrors.correction: Invite observations from defence, midfield, attack and interchange players.

commonErrors.error: Players list too many problems.
commonErrors.correction: Select the issue with the greatest match impact.

commonErrors.error: Feedback blames individuals without a solution.
commonErrors.correction: Describe the team behaviour and assign a constructive action.

commonErrors.error: The next block does not measure the adjustment.
commonErrors.correction: Set one observable success indicator before restarting.

progressions: Remove coaches from the review area.
Rotate leadership groups between blocks.
Use video clips during an extended post-session review.
Require written player self-assessments.
Conduct the process during a full match-length simulation.
regressions: Give leaders a structured review template.
Allow coaches to ask guiding questions.
Use one observation category only.
Shorten playing blocks.
Nominate the adjustment before the first review.
matchApplication: Mature teams solve problems on the ground and contribute meaningfully during breaks. This simulation develops shared tactical ownership rather than total dependence on coaches.
relatedDrills: MS-009 – Coach Observation and Feedback Simulation

title: Match Simulation Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Integrating all technical, tactical, physical, communication and decision-making requirements of match simulation.
objective: Complete a final assessment of the team’s ability to transfer the full Match Simulation chapter into realistic, continuous Australian football with minimal coach intervention.
groundSize: Full ground where available, or a proportionally reduced ground preserving normal positional and tactical relationships.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two balanced teams with interchange players.
Use normal positional structures, interchange procedures and coaching areas.
Establish a scoreboard and match clock.
Play two to four quarters according to player age, conditioning and session objectives.
Prepare scenario cards covering restarts, turnovers, score changes, tactical adjustments, environmental conditions and temporary player shortages.
Assign coaches and observers specific assessment categories.
Nominate player leadership groups.
Limit coach intervention to quarter breaks, safety issues and concise match-day messages.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin from a centre restart under normal match conditions.
Play continues as uninterrupted match simulation.
Coaches assess technical execution, structure, decision making, pressure, communication and leadership.
At selected natural breaks, the coach may introduce a realistic scenario condition.
Teams must recognise and respond using player-led organisation.
Interchanges and positional rotations occur live.
Quarter breaks follow a realistic review process.
The scoreboard and clock determine tactical requirements.
The final quarter includes a close-match scenario requiring independent player management.
Conclude with player self-assessment, line review and coach evaluation against the chapter success indicators.
coachingPoints: Players must apply previous chapter principles without waiting for drill-specific instructions.
Team structure should remain recognisable through attack, defence, transition and broken play.
Restarts and stoppages require rapid player-led organisation.
Possession, territory and risk must reflect score, time and field position.
Pressure should be connected, legal and purposeful.
Defensive and forward systems must remain balanced around turnovers.
Tactical adjustments should solve observed match problems.
Communication must occur across all positional lines.
Interchanges and emergencies must not create structural panic.
Coaches should assess transfer, consistency and adaptability rather than isolated highlights.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Team ball movement and line connection.

commonErrors.error: Players revert to individual football when pressure increases.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce team spacing, support and role discipline.

commonErrors.error: Structures work only when the starting scenario is announced.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and organise every naturally occurring match phase.

commonErrors.error: Tactical urgency removes turnover protection.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain connected players behind and around possession.

commonErrors.error: Coaches provide too much live direction.
commonErrors.correction: Allow players to identify and solve match problems.

commonErrors.error: Quarter-break feedback becomes excessive.
commonErrors.correction: Select the most important structural and behavioural priorities.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue reduces communication and legal technique.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify decisions, increase role calls and maintain safe execution.

progressions: Use independent or accredited umpires.
Play a full match-length simulation.
Give each team hidden tactical objectives.
Restrict coach communication to formal breaks.
Record the entire simulation for detailed review.
Invite external coaches to assess selected categories.
regressions: Play two shorter halves.
Use fewer scenario interventions.
Allow one coach stoppage per quarter.
Reduce contact for returning or mixed-ability players.
Provide player leaders with tactical reminder cards.
Use a reduced ground while preserving positional structure.
successIndicators: Maintain effective attacking and defensive structures.
Create purposeful forward entries and scoring opportunities.
Move the football through connected positional lines.
Adjust tempo, possession and risk to the match situation.
Recognise and respond to opposition tactics.
Manage interchanges and unexpected player losses.
Perform chapter principles in continuous match conditions.
matchApplication: This final assessment measures whether the Match Simulation chapter has transferred into complete football performance. It tests the team’s ability to combine structure, skill, pressure, decision making, communication, leadership and tactical adaptability under realistic match conditions.
relatedDrills: MS-050 – Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment
MS-070 – Team Ball Movement Phase Assessment
MS-080 – Team Ball Movement Development Stage Assessment
